The Dutch Golden Age. This refers to the seventeenth century, when the Dutch Republic, the Netherlands, became a global power of unprecedented prosperity and cultural efflorescence. Through merchant enterprise, naval dominance, and trade monopolies, the Dutch accumulated vast wealth and global territories. Simultaneously, Amsterdam became a center of banking, insurance, and stock trading, the first modern financial system. Artistically and intellectually, the era produced masterpieces by painters Rembrandt and Vermeer, advances in mathematics and optics, and a spirit of religious toleration that made the Dutch Republic an intellectual haven in an age of European religious conflict.

The Dutch Revolt from fifteen sixty-eight to sixteen forty-eight ended Spanish rule over the Low Countries, establishing the Dutch Republic, the United Provinces, as an independent Protestant nation and major European power. The Treaty of Westphalia in sixteen forty-eight formally recognized Dutch independence from Spain, solidifying the republic's status and ending the Thirty Years' War.

The Dutch East India Company, the Vereenigde Oost-Indische Compagnie or VOC, chartered in sixteen oh-two, became history's largest and most powerful trading enterprise, monopolizing European trade with the East Indies, amassing vast profits, and establishing Dutch colonial dominion across Asia. The Dutch West India Company, the Geoctrooieerde Westindische Compagnie or WIC, chartered in sixteen twenty-one, pursued trade and territorial conquest in the Americas and Africa, trading in sugar, slaves, and other commodities.

Amsterdam became the commercial hub of the world as a center of banking, insurance, stock trading, and the world's first stock exchange established in sixteen oh-two, establishing financial instruments and practices that defined modern capitalism. Dutch merchants and traders grew immensely wealthy through commerce, creating an affluent merchant class that patronized the arts and elevated Amsterdam to cultural prominence.

Painting flourished under the patronage of wealthy merchants as Rembrandt van Rijn created masterpieces of portraiture and biblical narrative. Johannes Vermeer painted intimate domestic scenes of extraordinary subtlety and light, and lesser masters produced thousands of paintings of landscapes, still lifes, and daily life. Religious tolerance in the Dutch Republic attracted intellectuals and refugees including René Descartes, who lived and published in Amsterdam, John Locke and other English exiles who found refuge there, and Jewish communities that thrived and contributed to intellectual and commercial life.

The Dutch Tulip Mania from sixteen thirty-four to sixteen thirty-seven saw speculative frenzy over rare tulip bulbs, creating enormous price bubbles and crashes, history's first recorded financial bubble. The Dutch invented the telescope and microscope, made advances in mathematics including decimal notation, and became leaders in navigation and cartography, supporting their mercantile dominance.
